full_judgment: 7. However, I have heard the learned advocates for both the parties at length and examined the judgment of both the courts below, the pleadings of both the parties and also the evidence adduced by them. In this suit it is admitted by both the parties that the predecessor of the defendant nos. 1 and 2 was one of the original owners of the suit land. It is also not disputed that defendant nos. 1 and 2 have been residing in the suit land since their predecessor's time. The plaintiffs case is that after becoming owner of the suit land they on the request of the defendant no. I gave her permission to continue residing in the suit land as a licensee under them. So it is evident that in this suit, to get a decree as prayed for the plaintiff must prove that he actually gave permission to the defendant nos. 1 and 2 to reside in this suit land as licensee under them. But it appears that the plaintiff could not adduce any evidence before the Court to prove this alleged fact. The plaintiff have adduced 3 witnesses including the plaintiff no. 1. This plaintiff no. 1 during cross examination, has admitted that he cannot say when the defendant took permission from him to reside in the suit land and that he has no evidence to prove that the defendants have been possessing the suit land as licensee under them. Rather this P.W. I during cross-examination has admitted that in R.S. Khatian of the suit land the names of the defendants have been recorded and lie did not raise any objection against that recording. This plaintiff has his a admitted that the defendants have been paying rent for the suit land. The other 3 witnesses of the plaintiff have stated in the cross examination that they cannot say how the defendants have been possessing the suit land. This P.Ws. though have stated that they heard that the defendants have been possessing the suit land on taking permission but could not say any details of that taking permission or even could not say from whom they heard about that taking permission. The learned trial court while decreeing the suit for eviction did not consider at all that the plaintiff could not adduce any cogent evidence before the Court to prove their case that the defendant nos. 1 and 2 have been possessing the suit land as permissive possessions. However, it appears that the appellate Court, on proper consideration and appreciation of evidence on record has rightly found that the plaintiffs have failed to adduce any documentary evidence or cogent oral evidence to prove their case of permissive possession. The appellate Court, on scrutiny of the evidence on record, has also found that the own documentary evidence of the plaintiff rather support the presumption that Abdus Subhan, the predecessor of the defendant 1 and 2 retained some land in his possession and the plaintiffs could not got possession of those land. However, where it is admitted that defendants 1 and 2 are the heirs of original owner of suit land and they are also in possession of the suit land continuously since their predecessor's time and where the records of right have been prepared in the name of the defendants and their predecessors and where the defendants have been paying rent for the suit land and where there is no cogent evidence to prove the plaintiffs case that the defendants 1 and 2 have been possessing the Suit land as license on taking permission from the plaintiff the trial court was not justified and correct at all to decree the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. The appellate Court therefore rightly reversed the judgment of the trial Court and rightly dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. I find legal infirmity in the judgment of the appellate Court.
